scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: A tiny jab today can protect you from a disease years later. How does your body remember?

scenes.name: antigen
scenes.text: A vaccine shows your body a harmless version of a germ. A weakened or killed germ, a piece of it, or instructions to make that piece.

scenes.name: detect
scenes.text: Immune cells spot this unfamiliar shape, called an antigen, and raise the alarm.

scenes.name: antibody
scenes.text: B cells start making antibodies, Y shaped proteins that lock onto that exact antigen, and mark it for destruction.

scenes.name: tcells
scenes.text: T cells join in. Some help coordinate the response, others learn to destroy infected cells.

scenes.name: memory
scenes.text: Afterwards, memory cells stay behind, often for years. If the real germ shows up, they react much faster and stronger, often before you get sick.

scenes.name: side
scenes.text: A sore arm or mild fever usually just means your immune system is busy training. And when many people are vaccinated, the germ struggles to spread.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Preview, alarm, antibodies, memory. Your body's training drill. Follow for more on how things really work.
